newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain says tariffs won't be used to cut deficit.
newsitem.headline: Spain says tariffs won't be used to cut deficit.

text.p: Spain's Economy Ministry denied on Friday that a portion of regulated tariffs on telephones, electricity, gas and petrol will go towards paying the public deficit next year.

"The state has asked (Spanish) industry for a contribution to lower inflation as long as this does not hurt corporate results but not to transfer part of their income to cut the deficit," an Economy Ministry spokesman said.

The stock market was down sharply this morning after an article in financial daily La Gaceta said that in the 1997 budget a part of the new tariffs would go to cut the deficit, but analysts dismissed the report as lacking in foundation.
Analysts said the article had an exaggerated impact, coming close on the heels of sustained losses in Gas Natural after the state raised gas prices by less than expected.
The implications were that regulated sectors would cease to be cushioned by the government via their pricing systems.
"It's picking up on the theme in a broader way," said one analyst. "We do expect the regulated side of the economy not to do as well over the next few years."
"The regulated sectors are going to come under pressure," said Eric Rovick, head of research at AB Asesores brokerage.
A trader said investors were becoming increasingly worried about the budget and the implications for the larger state-owned companies of the government's determination to fight inflation.
On a short-term basis, traders abroad were using this story as a way to take profits, he said.
Analysts said it was difficult to quantify what this might mean for stock prices as the period of uncertainty for some sectors, such as electricity companies, could last for some months.
New electricity charges are not usually announced until the end of the year, and there is also legislation pending for the sector, which analysts said was another risk factor.

Endesa, traditionally considered the most favoured among the state-participated electricity firms, could hit 6,880 pesetas, from around 7,140 pesetas after a poor performance so far this year, dealers said.
Telefonica, which was also down sharply today, "is a different story," according to Luis Broto, a salesman at BZW in Madrid.
"It's been holding up pretty well. Tariffs have already fallen a lot so far, so it's another case," he said.

Energy group Repsol, meanwhile, should be relatively protected from this new bout of jitters, mainly because the share price has fared so badly already this year. But still, Broto was not ruling out further downside.
Overall, the problem was one of poor sentiment on uncertainties overhanging Spanish companies, he said.

"The Spanish government has been very generous up to now, but in the fight against inflation, the most obvious thing to do is pull down the regulated tariffs. We've had hints about what's going to happen. It's going to get more and more competitive," he said. "Basically we're expecting greater risk."
